kept_issues.body:
## Summary

Add a `lazy` parameter to `@st.fragment` that defers fragment execution until the fragment's placeholder scrolls into the browser viewport. This is inspired by how Sigma Computing dashboards lazy-load visualizations — tiles below the fold don't execute their queries until the user scrolls them into view, dramatically reducing initial page load time for long dashboards.

## Proposed API

```python
@overload
def fragment(
    func: F,
    *,
    run_every: int | float | timedelta | str | None = None,
    parallel: bool = False,
    lazy: bool = False,
) -> F: ...
```

**Usage example:**

```python
@st.fragment(lazy=True)
def expensive_chart():
    data = fetch_from_database()  # only runs when scrolled into view
    st.line_chart(data)

# Top of page — runs immediately
summary_metrics()

# Below the fold — deferred until user scrolls down
expensive_chart()
another_expensive_section()
```

**Combined with parallel fragments:**

```python
@st.fragment(lazy=True, parallel=True)
def dashboard_card(query):
    data = run_query(query)
    st.metric(data["label"], data["value"])

# Visible row runs in parallel immediately
for q in visible_queries:
    dashboard_card(q)

# Below-the-fold row defers until scrolled into view,
# then runs its cards in parallel too
for q in more_queries:
    dashboard_card(q)
```

## Use cases

- **Long dashboard pages** with many SQL-backed sections — only the visible ones run queries on initial load, reducing total query cost and page load time.
- **Infinite-scroll-style apps** with many sections where most content is below the fold.

## Relationship to parallel fragments

Lazy fragments are **orthogonal** to `parallel=True` (#8490):

- **`lazy`** controls *when* a fragment enters the execution pipeline (immediately vs. on viewport visibility).
- **`parallel`** controls *how* scheduled fragments share the machine (sequential vs. concurrent threads).

Both can be `True` simultaneously. A dashboard's visible row of cards runs in parallel on initial load; the user scrolls down and the next row triggers lazily — and those should also run in parallel so they don't block each other.

## References

- #14277 — Parallel fragments product spec (where this idea was first discussed)
- #8490 — Parallel fragments feature request (104 reactions)
kept_issues.title: `st.fragment(lazy=True)` — defer fragment execution until visible (viewport-triggered loading)

 Summary

The new st.menu_button is a welcome addition. It would be more useful if it could be combined with download behavior: the user picks an export format from a menu (for example Markdown, plain text, or PDF), and Streamlit serves the matching file without requiring a separate st.download_button or fragile conditional wiring for each format.
The idea is a single control—similar to an Export menu in desktop apps—where each menu option is tied to download metadata (data, file_name, mime) so “choose format → file downloads” is a first-class pattern.

 Why?

Today, st.menu_button only communicates which option was selected on the rerun where the user picks something; sending bytes to the browser still requires st.download_button (or other workarounds). In practice that causes:
- Awkward UX: pick a format from the menu, then click again to download—or rely on st.session_state because the menu’s return value resets on later reruns.
- Repeated boilerplate: every app reimplements mapping from “format label” → data / file_name / mime.
- Cost vs. laziness: precomputing every variant (e.g. large PDFs or zips) wastes CPU and memory; deferring generation until after a choice fights Streamlit’s rerun model unless authors invent their own patterns.
A combined primitive would match common product UI, reduce custom session-state hacks, and make multi-format export easier to build and maintain.

 How?

Ship either a new widget (for example st.download_menu_button) or an extension of st.menu_button / st.download_button so one control can:
1. Show a dropdown of export labels.
2. On selection, trigger a download using the payload mapped to that label.
Options API (sketch for discussion)
Accept a structured mapping instead of plain string labels only, for example:
- A list of tuples or small dicts, e.g. (label, file_name, mime, data); or 
- A dict keyed by label with values like { "data": ..., "file_name": ..., "mime": ... }.
Lazy payloads
Allow data (or the equivalent field) to be a callable that Streamlit invokes only when that option is chosen, so expensive exports are not built on every rerun. Document when the callable runs, error handling, and any constraints (e.g. serialization, size limits).

 Additional Context

_No response_

I want the options to disable the "select all" button as argument to make the mulitselect component behave like previous versions

it makes the browser freeze

st.multiselect(label="large multi select", options=largeListOf165k, disableSelectAll=True)

### Additional Context

```python
 import time
    import streamlit as st
    st.title("Performance Defect: Cascading st.multiselect with Large Datasets")

    st.markdown("""
    ### Feature Request Context
    This example demonstrates a performance bottleneck involving two dependent `st.multiselect` widgets. 

    Selecting a category in the first widget filters the available choices in the second widget. When the underlying dataset contains 165,000 items, clicking the native **Select all** button on either widget triggers severe serialization overhead, memory spikes, and completely freezes the browser interface on a thinkpad p16 gen 1.

    **Requested Feature:** A configuration parameter to natively disable the "Select all" option (e.g., `show_select_all=False`).
    """)

    # Mock data: 3 groups, each containing 55,000 items (165k total rows)
    GROUPS = ["Group_A", "Group_B", "Group_C"]
    ITEMS_PER_GROUP = 55000

    # First widget: Select groups
    selected_groups = st.multiselect(
        label="1. Select Item Groups", options=GROUPS, default=["Group_A"]
    )

    # Generate dependent options based on the selection in the first widget
    available_options = []
    for group in selected_groups:
        available_options.extend([f"{group}_Item_{i}" for i in range(ITEMS_PER_GROUP)])

    # Second widget: Filtered choices based on the first widget
    # Clicking 'Select all' here on a large subset causes immediate UI failure
    selected_items = st.multiselect(
        label=f"2. Filtered Items (Current available choices: {len(available_options)})",
        options=available_options,
    )

    st.write(f"Total items selected in widget 2: {len(selected_items)}")

```

### Checklist

- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add support for `bind="query-params"` in `st.expander` and `st.popover`.

### Why?

I love both the new `bind="query-params"` feature, as well as the new "dynamic" `st.expander` (#13888), `st.tabs` (#13910), and `st.popover` (#13914) feature, and I'd like to use them together.

### How?

Support `bind="query-params"` in `st.expander()`, `st.tabs()`, and `st.popover()`.

### Additional Context

As a workaround for `st.tabs(bind="query-params")`, I have been using `st.segmented_control(bind="query-params")`, but it's not as nice visually.

For a while now, in my app, I hacked together a dynamic expander + query param, using a `st.button`. It works, but it's messy.
```py
from typing import Callable

import streamlit as st


def set_bool_query_param(key: str, value: bool):
    """Set a boolean query parameter in the URL."""
    if value:
        st.query_params[key] = value
    else:
        st.query_params.pop(key, None)


@st.fragment
def dynamic_expander(
    label: str,
    content: Callable,
    *,
    key: str,
    help: str | None = None,  # noqa: A002 Shadowing a Python builtin
):
    """Create an expander that only generates the content if it is expanded.

    Unlike `st.expander()`, which is a frontend component that always generates the content,
    this `dynamic_expander()` only generates the content if it is expanded.
    """
    expanded = key in st.query_params

    button = {
        "label": label,
        "help": help,
        "type": "tertiary",
        "icon": f":material/expand_{'less' if expanded else 'more'}:",
    }

    with st.container(border=True, key=key):
        placeholder = st.empty()
        if expanded:
            placeholder.button(key=f"{key}_button_disabled", disabled=True, **button)

            try:
                with st.spinner("Loading..."):
                    content()
            except Exception as e:
                st.exception(e)

        placeholder.button(
            key=f"{key}_button",
            on_click=set_bool_query_param,
            args=(key, not expanded),
            **button,
        )


def example():
    st.write("Content")


dynamic_expander("Example", example, key="example")
```

frontend/app/index.html hardcodes , regardless of the actual language of the app content. This causes browsers (e.g. Chrome) to detect a mismatch between the declared language and the page content, and show an unsolicited "Translate this page?" popup.

 

 Steps to Reproduce

1. Build a Streamlit app written entirely in Japanese (or any non-English language)
2. Open it in Chrome with the browser language set to Japanese
3. Chrome immediately shows a Google Translate prompt: "Translate from English?"

 Expected Behavior

No translation prompt appears, because the page language matches the content.

 Actual Behavior

Chrome shows a translation popup, since lang="en" signals that the page is English even when all content is Japanese.

(Screenshot to be attached)

 Root Cause

frontend/app/index.html line 18:

 

The React app (index.tsx) does not update document.documentElement.lang either.

 Proposed Solution

Expose a lang parameter in st.set_page_config() (or a dedicated config option), and have the server inject the value into the HTML at startup — similar to how is already customizable.

 

 Related

- Discuss thread: 
- Issue 1353 (i18n): 
- Issue 10380 (localization):

 Summary

Currently, st.date_input only supports continuous date ranges via min_value and max_value. 
There is no way to restrict selectable dates to a specific list of valid dates, such as 
dates available in a dataframe. Adding an allowed_dates parameter would fill this gap.

 Why?

I'm always frustrated when I need to show a date picker that only allows the user to select 
dates that exist in a dataset. For example, when a dataframe contains sales data only for 
specific dates, the current widget allows the user to select any date in the range, even 
dates with no data. This forces developers to use workarounds like st.selectbox, which 
lacks the calendar UI and date-picking experience that st.date_input provides.

 How?

Introduce a new parameter called allowed_dates in st.date_input with the following behavior:

- Accepts a list of datetime.date objects
- Disables all dates not present in the list in the calendar UI
- Example usage:

import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"date": ["2025-01-01", "2025-01-15", "2025-02-10"]})
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"]).dt.date

selected = st.date_input(
 "Select a date",
 allowed_dates=df["date"].tolist()
)

 Additional Context

This feature request was inspired by a common use case discussed while using st.date_input with dataframes. The current workaround is to use st.selectbox with the list of available dates, but this sacrifices the calendar UI experience.

Related issue: st.date_input currently supports min_value and max_value for continuous 
ranges, but has no support for non-continuous date lists.

    *,

    height: "content" | "stretch" | int = "content",

 Summary

Add a type parameter to st.radio with a "cards" variant that renders each option as a bordered, selectable card (with the selected card highlighted) instead of the default radio-button list. Same widget behavior — only the visual style changes. See Tremor's Radio Card Group for the look.

 Why?

Card-style single-select is a very common, more prominent and touch-friendly pattern for choosing between a few richer options (e.g. plans, payment methods, layouts, modes). Today users approximate it with columns + bordered containers + buttons/st.radio and a lot of manual state/CSS work. A built-in "cards" variant makes this polished pattern a one-liner.

 How?

Add a type parameter (default preserves today's look):

 

- type="default" — current radio-button list.
- type="cards" — render each option as a bordered card; the selected option is visually highlighted.
- Keep existing params working (captions, horizontal, format_func, index=None, etc.). Captions map naturally to a description line inside each card.

Alternative solution — a border: bool parameter: Instead of a type enum, just add st.radio(..., border=True) that wraps each option in a bordered card. This mirrors the border parameter on st.container and keeps the API minimal. Downside: it's less extensible than a type enum if we later want more visual variants (e.g. "pills"), and it's a boolean rather than a named style.

 Additional Context

- Reference designs:
 - Tremor — Radio Card Group
 - Tailwind Plus — Radio Groups (card designs)
 - streamlit-extras — Card Selector (existing community implementation)
- Related: 2325 (st.radio with sections), 7184 (stretch horizontal radio), 11959 (consistent API for selectbox/pills/segmented_control/radio).

 Summary

Refresh Streamlit's built-in default light and dark themes to feel more modern and polished out of the box — updated colors, typography, spacing, radii, and component styling — so that apps look great by default without custom theming.

 Why?

The default look is what every new app and most demos ship with, so it strongly shapes the perception of Streamlit. The current defaults feel somewhat dated compared to modern design systems (e.g. shadcn, Tailwind, Tremor, Material 3). A refreshed, cohesive default theme would make apps look more professional immediately, improve the first impression for new users, and reduce how often people reach for custom CSS/themes just to look current.

 How?

Revisit the default theme tokens and component styling for both light and dark modes, for example:

- Color palette: refined neutrals/grays, a more modern primary color, and better semantic colors (success/warning/error/info) with good contrast in both modes.
- Dark mode: ensure it's a first-class, well-balanced theme (not just an inversion) — proper surface elevations, borders, and contrast.
- Typography: modern default font, refined sizes/weights/line-heights and hierarchy.
- Spacing & shape: consistent spacing scale and slightly softer, contemporary border radii and borders.
- Components: cohesive styling across widgets, containers, dataframes, charts, etc.

Considerations:
- Accessibility: maintain/improve WCAG contrast in both themes.
- Backwards compatibility: this changes the look of existing apps, so consider how to roll it out (e.g. a new theme version/opt-in, migration notes) to avoid surprising users.
- Keep it fully overridable via the existing [theme] config.

 Additional Context

- Inspiration: modern design systems like shadcn/ui, Tailwind, Tremor, and Material 3.

 Summary

Add a first-party, Playwright-based end-to-end (browser) testing API for Streamlit apps — streamlit.testing.e2e — as an optional streamlit[testing] extra, complementing the existing browserless unit-testing API (AppTest). It would provide a Streamlit-aware semantic facade for finding and operating elements in a real browser, rerun/navigation-aware synchronization, useful failure artifacts, and an escape hatch to native Playwright Page/Locator. Design thoughts are in the app testing toolkit spec (PR 16041).

 Why?

Today users face an unhelpful choice: AppTest is fast and Python-native but runs no real frontend (so it can disagree with a real app, and can't cover rendering, custom components, accessibility, media, charts, or real user journeys), while browser testing can validate the real product but Streamlit provides no supported way to start the app, wait for reruns, select elements, collect logs, or test a deployed/embedded app — users must assemble and maintain all that infrastructure. Streamlit's own mature e2e_playwright/ suite solves these hard problems (process lifecycle, ephemeral ports, app-idle detection, traces, iframes, uploads, dataframes/charts, etc.) but is coupled to the repo layout and private DOM test IDs, so it isn't a releasable public API.

This is especially costly for AI coding agents, which need a deterministic run command, semantic element identity, a compact description of the current UI, and actionable failure artifacts to validate their work — indexes, private CSS/test IDs, sleeps, and screenshots alone make brittle tests.

 How?

Ship a two-layer testing story with clear boundaries (don't build a third UI-testing engine, and don't turn AppTest into a browser emulator):

- AppTest (browserless) stays the fast option for logic/state/basic widget workflows — with improved runtime fidelity and typed + universal semantic queries (get_by_key/get_by_label/get_by_text) and a compact snapshot().
- streamlit.testing.e2e (browser) — the new Playwright-based API, installed via pip install "streamlit[testing]".

Proposed shape (from the spec):

 

Key capabilities:
- App lifecycle fixture: app_fixture() starts one app server per test module on an ephemeral localhost port, gives an isolated browser page per test, and waits until the initial run is idle. Also target direct/external URLs (deployed/embedded apps).
- Semantic selection: strict, retrying finders that understand Streamlit elements and layout containers — get_element_by_key / get_element_by_label / get_element_by_text, plus get_element(type=...) / get_elements(type=...); a returned element that is a container (sidebar, form, expander, popover, dialog, tab, column, container) can scope further queries. An optional type discriminator maps to a generated public ElementType taxonomy for IDE completion.
- Rerun/navigation-aware synchronization so tests don't rely on sleeps.
- Actionable failure artifacts (text/logs/traces/screenshots) and a semantic snapshot (semantic_snapshot()) as a token-efficient interface for humans and agents.
- Escape hatch to native Playwright Page/Locator for anything the facade doesn't cover.
- A shared testability vocabulary across both layers (public element types, labels, keys, containers), explicitly optimized for AI agents.

 Additional Context

- Spec: [PR 16041 — \[spec] Streamlit app testing toolkit\]( (specs/2026-07-16-streamlit-app-testing-toolkit/product-spec.md).
- Related: open feature:app-testing issues, e.g. 9786, 13163, 9128.

It would provide a Streamlit-aware semantic facade for finding and operating elements in a real browser, rerun/navigation-aware synchronization, useful failure artifacts, and an escape hatch to native Playwright `Page`/`Locator`. Design thoughts are in the [app testing toolkit spec (PR #16041)](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16041).

### Why?

Today users face an unhelpful choice: `AppTest` is fast and Python-native but runs no real frontend (so it can disagree with a real app, and can't cover rendering, custom components, accessibility, media, charts, or real user journeys), while browser testing can validate the real product but Streamlit provides **no supported way** to start the app, wait for reruns, select elements, collect logs, or test a deployed/embedded app — users must assemble and maintain all that infrastructure. Streamlit's own mature `e2e_playwright/` suite solves these hard problems (process lifecycle, ephemeral ports, app-idle detection, traces, iframes, uploads, dataframes/charts, etc.) but is coupled to the repo layout and private DOM test IDs, so it isn't a releasable public API.

This is especially costly for **AI coding agents**, which need a deterministic run command, semantic element identity, a compact description of the current UI, and actionable failure artifacts to validate their work — indexes, private CSS/test IDs, sleeps, and screenshots alone make brittle tests.

### How?

Ship a two-layer testing story with clear boundaries (don't build a third UI-testing engine, and don't turn AppTest into a browser emulator):

- **AppTest (browserless)** stays the fast option for logic/state/basic widget workflows — with improved runtime fidelity and typed + universal semantic queries (`get_by_key`/`get_by_label`/`get_by_text`) and a compact `snapshot()`.
- **`streamlit.testing.e2e` (browser)** — the new Playwright-based API, installed via `pip install "streamlit[testing]"`.

Proposed shape (from the spec):

```python
from playwright.sync_api import expect
from streamlit.testing.e2e import StreamlitPage, app_fixture

app = app_fixture("app.py")

def test_sign_in(app: StreamlitPage):
    app.get_element_by_label("Username", type="text_input").set_value("ada")
    app.get_element_by_label("Password", type="text_input").set_value("correct horse battery staple")
    app.get_element_by_label("Sign in", type="button").click()

    welcome = app.get_element_by_text("Welcome, ada", type="heading")
    expect(welcome.locator).to_be_visible()
```

Key capabilities:
- **App lifecycle fixture:** `app_fixture()` starts one app server per test module on an ephemeral localhost port, gives an isolated browser page per test, and waits until the initial run is idle. Also target direct/external URLs (deployed/embedded apps).
- **Semantic selection:** strict, retrying finders that understand Streamlit elements and layout containers — `get_element_by_key` / `get_element_by_label` / `get_element_by_text`, plus `get_element(type=...)` / `get_elements(type=...)`; a returned element that is a container (sidebar, form, expander, popover, dialog, tab, column, container) can scope further queries. An optional `type` discriminator maps to a generated public `ElementType` taxonomy for IDE completion.
- **Rerun/navigation-aware synchronization** so tests don't rely on sleeps.
- **Actionable failure artifacts** (text/logs/traces/screenshots) and a **semantic snapshot** (`semantic_snapshot()`) as a token-efficient interface for humans and agents.
- **Escape hatch** to native Playwright `Page`/`Locator` for anything the facade doesn't cover.
- A shared **testability vocabulary** across both layers (public element types, labels, keys, containers), explicitly optimized for AI agents.

### Additional Context

- Spec: [PR #16041 — \`[spec] Streamlit app testing toolkit\`](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/pull/16041) (`specs/2026-07-16-streamlit-app-testing-toolkit/product-spec.md`).
- Related: open `feature:app-testing` issues, e.g. #9786, #13163, #9128.
kept_issues.title: Add a first-party Playwright-based e2e testing API (`streamlit.testing.e2e`) alongside AppTest

 Summary

Deprecate the persist parameter of st.cache_data (persist="disk"). It doesn't fit well with the rest of the API and is incompatible with more recent features. A better, more flexible alternative is to make the cache storage backend configurable (e.g. via st.App), so users can plug in a storage that persists to disk — or Redis/S3 — consistently across the whole app.

 Why?

persist="disk" is a narrow, awkward escape hatch:
- It only supports a single hardcoded mode ("disk") with a non-configurable location (3018).
- It doesn't compose cleanly with other cache features — e.g. it ignores ttl (4859).
- It's a per-function flag for what is really a deployment/storage concern, so it's easy to misuse and inconsistent across an app.
- It doesn't scale to multi-instance deployments (each replica has its own local disk), where users actually want a shared/central store.

A configurable storage backend addresses all of this in one coherent mechanism, and persistence becomes just one storage implementation rather than a special-cased parameter.

 How?

- Introduce a configurable cache storage API (per the custom storage API spec, PR 14902) — e.g. a cache_storage_manager parameter on st.App — that lets users supply a custom backend (disk, Redis, S3, …) applied consistently to st.cache_data.
 - A built-in/example disk-persisting storage would cover today's persist="disk" use case (with configurable location, and without the ttl incompatibility).
- Deprecate persist on st.cache_data with a long, clearly-communicated window and a documented migration path (it keeps working during deprecation). Follow "Graceful Evolution" — 3+ months notice, clear migration guidance.

 Additional Context

- Docs: st.cache_data.
- Replacement direction: PR 14902 — custom storage API for st.App (also motivated by 5849 "bring your own Redis cache").
- Related persist limitations: 4859 (persist='disk' ignores ttl), 3018 (configurable location for persistent cache).

 Summary

Add an opt-in copy="cow" mode to st.cache_data that uses copy-on-write semantics for cached return values. This avoids unnecessary full-object deserialization on cache hits while preserving isolation between callers, significantly reducing cache-hit latency and memory allocation for large cached objects.

 Why?

st.cache_data currently creates an independent copy of the cached value for each call. This provides isolation between callers, but for large objects such as Pandas DataFrames and NumPy arrays, repeatedly deserializing and copying cached values can introduce significant CPU time and memory allocation overhead.

This becomes particularly relevant for applications where large datasets are read repeatedly across multiple sessions, while mutations to returned values are relatively uncommon.

An opt-in copy-on-write mode can preserve the isolation guarantees of st.cache_data while avoiding unnecessary full-object duplication on cache hits. The existing behavior would remain unchanged for applications that do not opt into the new mode.

In benchmarks using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0, the prototype reduced observed cache-hit latency by approximately 2.7–3.2× for DataFrames ranging from 5,000 to 1,000,000 rows. In a separate allocation benchmark with 10 consecutive reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB to 0.02–0.03 MB.

 How?

Introduce an optional copy parameter on st.cache_data:

python
@st.cache_data(copy="cow")
def load_data():
 return pd.read_parquet("large_dataset.parquet")

 Additional Context

 Prototype

A working prototype is available in my fork:

 

The implementation is currently limited to the following areas:

- st.cache_data API support for copy="cow"
- Copy-on-write handling for supported cached return values
- Caller/session mutation isolation
- Integration with existing cache lifecycle and eviction behavior
- Unit tests for mutation isolation
- Static typing coverage for the public API

 Performance Benchmark

The prototype was benchmarked using Python 3.13.15, Pandas 3.0.6, and Streamlit 1.64.0.

| Dataset | Default copy | copy="cow" | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 × 12 | 0.155 ms | 0.055 ms | 2.8× |
| 50,000 × 12 | 0.158 ms | 0.049 ms | 3.2× |
| 200,000 × 12 | 0.144 ms | 0.048 ms | 3.0× |
| 1,000,000 × 12 | 0.131 ms | 0.049 ms | 2.7× |

In a separate allocation benchmark using 10 consecutive cache reads, observed allocation decreased from approximately 4.67 MB with the existing behavior to approximately 0.02–0.03 MB with copy="cow".

 Stress Testing

The implementation was also tested under concurrent mutation and cache lifecycle pressure:

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| 50 concurrent threads mutating the same 100,000-row DataFrame | Passed |
| Nested dictionaries containing DataFrames, Series, and lists | Passed |
| 200 concurrent cache entries with max_entries=5 | Passed |
| Concurrent readers while repeatedly calling .clear() | Passed |
| 1,000,000-row (~100 MB) DataFrame with mutation isolation | Passed |

The concurrent mutation test completed in approximately 0.046 seconds. The cached DataFrame remained unchanged and no cross-caller mutations were observed.

The 1,000,000-row test also preserved mutation isolation, with subsequent reads completing in approximately 0.08 ms.

These tests were specifically designed to validate both the performance characteristics and the isolation guarantees of the proposed copy-on-write behavior.

 Summary

Start downloading the Material Symbols icon font while the page loads, instead of waiting until the first icon renders. Icons are part of the app's own UI and of many apps, so on a first (uncached) visit they often appear late, with visible loading artifacts until the font has downloaded.

 Why?

Material icons are now a common part of most apps:

- Streamlit's own UI uses them: the sidebar collapse and expand buttons, the main menu items, and the status widget.
- Many apps use them for page icons in st.navigation / st.Page, icon= on buttons, expanders, alerts and toasts, and :material/...: in Markdown.

The font is declared in frontend/app/src/assets/css/fonts.css with font-display: block and is about 375 KB. Browsers request an @font-face font only once text using it is laid out, so the download starts only after the JS bundle has run, the websocket has connected and the first icon has rendered. Until the font arrives, icons render as blank space. On slow connections, once the browser's block period (about 3 seconds) ends, the fallback font shows the icon's ligature name (for example keyboard_double_arrow_left) instead. Later visits hit the browser cache, so this mostly affects first loads, which is what new users see.

 How?

Start the download from the app's entry script with the CSS Font Loading API, instead of waiting for the first icon to render:

 

This needs no file name, so it can't go stale, and because it runs once the entry bundle has loaded, it doesn't compete with the JS the app needs for its first render.

Alternatives considered:

- A in index.html, as we do for Source Sans. That preload hard-codes the font's hashed file name, which works because Source Sans rarely changes. The update-emojis-material-icons workflow replaces the Material Symbols font every few weeks (28 times in 2026 so far), and each update changes its hash. Only the Vite build can compute that name, so a hard-coded preload would silently go stale. Keeping it current would need a build-time index.html transform or a frontend build inside the update script.
- fetchpriority="low" on such a preload would start the download even earlier, but it can't keep the font from competing with the JS. Over HTTP/1.1, the hint only delays when the request is sent, and the download then shares bandwidth.

The trade-off: every first visit downloads the font, even for apps that never show an icon.

 Summary

Add an icon parameter to st.selectbox that shows an emoji or Material icon inside the input field, to the left of the selected value. st.text_input (10761) and st.number_input (10711) already support this, which came from 8787.

 Why?

An icon hints at what the field is for (a globe for a country, a person for an assignee, a calendar for a reporting period) and lets a selectbox line up visually with text and number inputs that already have icons in the same form.

Today the only workaround is prefixing every option with an emoji via format_func. That repeats the icon in every dropdown row, changes the displayed value, and can't use Material icons (12151).

 How?

Match the existing icon parameter on st.text_input and st.number_input:

 

- icon: str | None = None. Accepts a single-character emoji, ":material/icon_name:", or "spinner", validated with validate_icon_or_emoji and documented with the same docstring as the other inputs.
- The icon renders at the start of the input field, before the selected value or placeholder. It stays visible while the user types to filter options, with accept_new_options=True, and when the widget is disabled.
- Size, spacing, and color match the start icon of st.text_input / st.number_input (StyledStartEnhancer), so the three widgets align when stacked.
- As with the other inputs, icon is part of the widget ID only when no key is set.

 Additional Context

- Original request for input icons: 8787.

### Checklist

- [x] I have searched the [existing issues](https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues) for similar feature requests.
- [x] I added a descriptive title and summary to this issue.

### Summary

Add an `icon` parameter to `st.selectbox` that shows an emoji or Material icon inside the input field, to the left of the selected value. `st.text_input` (#10761) and `st.number_input` (#10711) already support this, which came from #8787.

### Why?

An icon hints at what the field is for (a globe for a country, a person for an assignee, a calendar for a reporting period) and lets a selectbox line up visually with text and number inputs that already have icons in the same form.

Today the only workaround is prefixing every option with an emoji via `format_func`. That repeats the icon in every dropdown row, changes the displayed value, and can't use Material icons (#12151).

### How?

Match the existing `icon` parameter on `st.text_input` and `st.number_input`:

```python
country = st.selectbox("Country", countries, icon=":material/public:")
assignee = st.selectbox("Assignee", people, icon="👤", placeholder="Pick someone")
```

- `icon: str | None = None`. Accepts a single-character emoji, `":material/icon_name:"`, or `"spinner"`, validated with `validate_icon_or_emoji` and documented with the same docstring as the other inputs.
- The icon renders at the start of the input field, before the selected value or placeholder. It stays visible while the user types to filter options, with `accept_new_options=True`, and when the widget is disabled.
- Size, spacing, and color match the start icon of `st.text_input` / `st.number_input` (`StyledStartEnhancer`), so the three widgets align when stacked.
- As with the other inputs, `icon` is part of the widget ID only when no `key` is set.

### Additional Context

- Original request for input icons: #8787.
- Related but separate: icons and Markdown inside option labels (#12151, #7466).
- `st.multiselect`, `st.date_input`, and `st.time_input` could get the same parameter later; this issue covers `st.selectbox` only.
kept_issues.title: Add `icon` parameter to `st.selectbox`
